note: Context-fit rules used by the guided assessment. These are AI-authored editorial judgements about which tools serve which kind of work, and they are unreviewed. They deliberately live in content rather than code so a reviewer can audit them. Repository signals do not contribute to any rule here. Learner candidates are additionally gated by a stated baseline so that someone new to HTML and CSS is not handed an application toolchain. Review status is tracked per rule (rule_id), not per file: approving one rule must never publish an unrelated one.

sass.text: Still fine where it already exists. A working stylesheet is an asset; migrating it wholesale rarely pays for itself.

bootstrap.text: Reasonable to keep on an existing internal or admin interface. Replacing it is a redesign, not an upgrade.

npm.text: No reason to change package manager purely for its own sake on a codebase you are maintaining.

gulp.text: The bundler now owns the dependency graph that Gulp used to orchestrate. Keeping it means maintaining a plugin chain that newer tooling makes unnecessary.

grunt.text: Superseded by Gulp and then by bundlers. A Gruntfile is usually the oldest thing in a repository.

jquery.text: Most of what it was used for is now native: querySelectorAll, classList, fetch. It is often the easiest dependency to remove outright.

bower.text: Deprecated by its own maintainers and the registry is effectively frozen — no security advisories will reach you.

angularjs.text: End of life since 2022 and receives no security patches. On anything handling user data this is a risk, not a preference.

webpack.text: Still capable, but if the dev-server wait is part of your daily cost, that cost is now avoidable.

candidates.why: You are maintaining a build that predates bundlers owning the dependency graph. Vite is the smallest step that removes the plugin chain and the dev-server wait at the same time.
candidates.unsuitable_if: Your build depends on webpack-specific loaders or module federation with no Vite equivalent — check before committing to a migration.

candidates.why: You marked jQuery. htmx lets you keep server-rendered pages and drop the jQuery dependency without adopting a client-side framework — the smaller of the two available moves.
candidates.unsuitable_if: The application has genuinely rich client state — an editor, a canvas, real-time collaboration — in which case a framework is the right answer, not htmx.

candidates.why: TypeScript can make unfamiliar JavaScript code easier to navigate and change by providing type information, reference checking, and editor-assisted refactoring.
candidates.unsuitable_if: The codebase is small enough to maintain safely without it, the team cannot sustain type coverage, or the migration itself creates more risk than it resolves. Incremental TypeScript adoption in a large untyped codebase should be treated as a migration project, not merely a configuration change.

candidates.why: On an older repository with a large dependency tree, the strict layout surfaces undeclared dependencies that npm silently tolerates — a common source of surprise during a migration.
candidates.unsuitable_if: Packages in your tree rely on a flat, permissive node_modules layout.

candidates.why: Legacy maintenance is mostly reading unfamiliar code and making mechanical changes across many files, which is the shape of work agentic tools handle best.
candidates.unsuitable_if: Your organisation cannot send source code to a third-party service.

sass.text: Fine for content sites, though check how much of what you use is now native CSS.

bootstrap.text: Defensible when you need a working layout faster than a distinctive one.

tailwind.text: Works well here — content sites usually have few enough templates that utility classes stay manageable.

nextjs.text: For a content site this is often more rendering machinery than the job needs.

react.text: A content site rarely needs a client-side framework runtime shipped to every visitor.

webpack.text: Heavier than a content build requires.

candidates.why: You build content sites. Astro ships zero JavaScript by default and lets you opt into interactivity per component — the inverse of the framework assumption, and the right default for content.
candidates.unsuitable_if: The site is really an application in disguise, with pervasive client state across most of the page.

candidates.why: Content sites have a small number of templates, so a fixed token scale gives you consistency without building a design system first.
candidates.unsuitable_if: Non-developers edit the templates without running the build, or the markup must stay framework-neutral for third parties.

candidates.why: For a simple new stack this is the least you can adopt and still get a fast modern build.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are using a framework that brings its own build and adding Vite separately would duplicate it.

candidates.why: Content work involves a lot of repetitive template and copy editing, which is where editor-integrated assistance pays off most directly.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are committed to an editor other than VS Code, or cannot send source to a third party.

react.text: A reasonable default for application work, and the largest hiring pool.

vite.text: The current default build for application work.

typescript.text: Retain TypeScript when the application already depends on its type checking, typed APIs, or TypeScript-based tooling. Removing it may discard useful type information and require changes across the codebase.

tailwind.text: Works well in component-based application code.

jquery.text: In an application codebase this usually indicates a layer nobody has revisited.

webpack.text: Capable, but the dev-server cost is now avoidable.

styled-components.text: Runtime CSS-in-JS fits server rendering poorly and costs render performance.

jest.text: If you already build with Vite, a second build configuration for tests is avoidable.

candidates.why: For an application maintained by several people, TypeScript can improve editor-assisted navigation, rename operations, and reference checking during changes.
candidates.unsuitable_if: The application is a short-lived prototype, the team does not intend to maintain type coverage, or introducing TypeScript would add more complexity than the project warrants.

candidates.why: You already build with Vite, so tests can share that configuration instead of maintaining a second one.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are on React Native, where Jest remains better supported.

candidates.why: Most application state turns out to be a cache of server data. Naming that distinction removes a lot of hand-written loading and refetch logic.
candidates.unsuitable_if: Your state is genuinely client-side — editor buffers, form drafts — or your framework already provides a data layer.

candidates.why: Application work is where end-to-end coverage matters most, and auto-waiting removes the flakiness that usually kills these suites.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You have no capacity to maintain an E2E suite — an ignored suite is worse than none.

candidates.why: Application changes usually span several files and need tests run between steps, which is the shape of task an agentic tool handles.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You cannot send source code to a third-party service.

storybook.text: The right tool for this work — it is where a design system crosses a team boundary.

sass.text: Mixins and compile-time logic are one of the few remaining cases with no native equivalent, and design systems are that case.

typescript.text: Retain TypeScript when the design system publishes type information that consuming applications rely on. Removing it may break editor support or require consumers to recreate those types.

figma.text: Where the tokens you are implementing usually originate.

tailwind.text: Components consumed by other teams generally need to emit semantic, restyleable markup. Utility classes in a shared library push your styling decisions into their markup.

bootstrap.text: A design system usually exists precisely because an off-the-shelf component set was not distinctive enough.

styled-components.text: Runtime styling in a shared library imposes its cost on every consumer.

candidates.why: You build components other people consume. CSS Modules give you scoping while emitting ordinary, restyleable CSS — which matters when the consumer needs to override you.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You need a shared token scale supplied for you rather than authored, in which case a framework is the better fit.

candidates.why: Querying by accessible role is doubly useful in a component library: the tests survive refactors, and a component you cannot query by role is usually one a screen reader cannot navigate.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are testing genuinely internal logic, which belongs in plain unit tests.

candidates.why: A component library can reduce integration effort by publishing usable type information with its public APIs.
candidates.unsuitable_if: The library already provides accurate and maintained type information through JSDoc or generated declarations, and changing the implementation would add cost without improving the consumer experience.

candidates.why: Component libraries benefit from visual and interaction coverage across engines, since you cannot control which browser a consumer targets.
candidates.unsuitable_if: Your CI cannot run browser binaries.

angularjs.text: End of life. Learning it now teaches you a framework you will only ever encounter in maintenance.

bower.text: Deprecated. Any tutorial teaching it is at least eight years old, and so is everything else in it.

grunt.text: Superseded twice over. Useful to recognise, not to learn.

candidates.why: You are comfortable with static pages. Sass is the smallest step beyond plain CSS that teaches you why build steps exist at all, without committing you to a framework.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You would rather learn what modern CSS does natively first — which is a defensible choice, since much of what Sass added is now built in.

candidates.why: You already write JavaScript. Vite is the current default build tool and needs almost no configuration, so you can learn it without learning build engineering first.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are following a course built around a different toolchain — fighting the course is not worth it.

candidates.why: Once a learner is comfortable writing JavaScript and has built an application, TypeScript can introduce static type checking and type-aware editor tooling without replacing the need to understand JavaScript.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are still developing fluency in HTML, CSS, or JavaScript. In that case, learning the frontend fundamentals first may reduce unnecessary cognitive load.

candidates.why: You have already built a frontend application. React is not necessarily the best framework, but it is the one most tutorials, libraries and job listings assume, which makes everything else easier to read.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are drawn to a simpler model — Vue and Svelte are gentler and the concepts transfer.

candidates.why: Worth learning deliberately rather than by osmosis — including where it misleads you, which matters more while you are still building judgement.
candidates.unsuitable_if: You are learning fundamentals and would accept generated code you cannot yet evaluate. That is the main trap.
